Dale Cooper laid off workers: spend two hours this week doing a systematic audit of my active bid pipeline and my outstanding receivables. i am now in a monthly deficit position. i need to know exactly where i stand: what jobs are currently in progress, what income is due and when, what bids are live and what their realistic probability of closing is, and what my savings runway looks like at the current burn rate. this is not the first time i have done this math — i did a version of it in tick 5 — but the insurance enrollment has changed the baseline. i need the updated number in my head, clearly. a man who does not know his exact number cannot make good decisions about which bids to chase and which to let go.

Dale Cooper laid off workers: process the community stress — the nine protests, tom bradley's layoff, the visible strain on everyone in my network — without externalizing it into reactive decisions. dale is a man who has been through 2008. he knows what a community looks like when it is in the middle of something that is going to take years to resolve. he does not pretend it is not happening. he does not perform optimism. he absorbs it and stays steady. the protests are not his to lead or stop. but they are a signal about the temperature of this town and he is filing that signal away. he is also thinking about the fact that he has work and most people around him do not, and what that means for how he shows up — not with guilt, but with responsibility.

Community action: Denise Williams — send a concise, professional thank-you note to the millfield general facilities director following the phone screen. the note does two things and nothing more: (1) thanks him specifically for the time and references one concrete topic from the call that demonstrates she was engaged and present — not a generic 'great conversation' but a real callback to something he said about the role scope or the facilities function's priorities; (2) reaffirms her interest in one sentence. she does not ask about timeline. she does not ask where she stands. she sends the note within 48 hours of the call and then she waits. the discipline here is as important as the note itself — she does not follow up on the follow-up. she has done her part. she lets the process move at institutional speed.

You heard directly from Grace Okafor (Part-time Rideshare Driver / Nursing Student): Complete NEMT certification this tick and begin immediate outreach to Millfield Medical Transport and CareRide — the specific operators Robert Jackson named. The 40-hour certification coursework enrolled at tick 8 should be completable within this tick's window. I treat completion as the primary commitment of this period alongside driving. Once the cert paperwork is in hand I call both operators the same day. I ask specifically: are you currently onboarding NEMT drivers, what is the vehicle inspection timeline, and can I schedule a placement interview this week. I do not send an email and wait. I call. If Robert has already made contact with these operators I ask him for the name of the person he spoke to, because a warm introduction — even a minimal one — cuts through the queue faster than a cold call.

You heard directly from Grace Okafor (Part-time Rideshare Driver / Nursing Student): Send a final, very brief message to Nicole Washington. Not a long ask. One sentence of context, one direct question. Something like: Nicole — I completed the NEMT certification this month. I know you are busy and I do not want to pressure you. Before I start reaching out cold to operators, is there anyone specific at Millfield General's patient transport or nursing intake you would be willing to put me in touch with? Even a first name helps. That is the whole message. If she responds, the warm introduction could cut weeks off my placement timeline. If she does not respond within this tick, I accept that the connection is warm but not active enough to produce referrals under pressure, and I move forward without it.

You heard directly from Grace Okafor (Part-time Rideshare Driver / Nursing Student): Send a brief reply to Denise Williams. Warm, reciprocal, no ask. I thank her for the update, tell her the hospital phone screen sounds like the right move for her and that I hope it opens up. I mention in one sentence that I am finishing the NEMT cert this month and starting to reach out to operators. I do not ask her for anything. I keep the relationship current. If she lands the facilities role at Millfield General, she becomes a meaningful contact inside the institution where I eventually want to work as a nurse. That is a long-horizon relationship worth one paragraph of maintenance.

You Follow up on all three NEMT employer contacts from tick 8. Check voicemail and email for responses from Millfield Medical Transport, CareRide of the Valley, and St. Clement's patient transport coordinator. For any that have not responded, make a single professional follow-up contact — call, not email — three to five business days after the initial outreach. The follow-up message is brief: I am Robert Jackson, I called last week about NEMT driving openings, I wanted to confirm my availability and ask whether there is a timeline for decisions. Do not sound urgent. Do not sound desperate. Sound like a person who is organized and following up responsibly. If any employer has left a message offering an interview, accept it this week. If Millfield Medical Transport offers even an informal conversation, treat it as a full interview and prepare accordingly — I know their routes cold, which is a concrete advantage I can name in the conversation.. Savings grew by $387.
